walkthroughs.body_html:
Fundamentals Of Communication & Networking — a core area of A-Level Computer Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Fundamentals Of Communication & Networking brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Fundamentals Of Communication & Networking.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: In the TCP/IP stack, which layer is responsible for routing packets between different networks?
options: Application layer
Link layer
Network (internet) layer
Transport layer

mcqs.q: A protocol is best described as:
options: A type of network cable
An agreed set of rules governing communication between devices
A program that deletes packets
The physical layout of a network

mcqs.q: In packet switching, the packets of one message:
options: Must all follow exactly the same route
Are always delivered in the order sent
May take different routes and are reassembled at the destination
Are merged into a single continuous stream before sending

mcqs.q: Which statement about IP and MAC addresses is correct?
options: A MAC address is fixed to the hardware; an IP address is logical and can change
Both are assigned permanently at manufacture
An IP address identifies the network card hardware
MAC addresses are used to route packets across the internet

mcqs.q: Is bandwidth the speed at which data travels along the cable?
options: Yes - higher bandwidth means each bit physically moves faster.
Yes - packets are chained together so they cannot separate.
No - bandwidth is the capacity of the channel (bits per second it can carry); the travel delay of a signal is latency, a separate measure.
Yes - bandwidth is measured in metres per second.

mcqs.q: Does a device keep the same IP address forever?
options: Yes - every device's IP address is burned in at manufacture.
Yes - bandwidth is measured in metres per second.
No - IP addresses are logical and commonly assigned dynamically (e.g. by DHCP), so they can change; the MAC address is the fixed hardware identifier.
Yes - changing an IP address is impossible without a new device.

mcqs.q: Do the packets of a message always arrive in the order they were sent?
options: Yes - changing an IP address is impossible without a new device.
No - packets may travel different routes and arrive out of order; sequence numbers let the receiving end reassemble them correctly.
Yes - packets are chained together so they cannot separate.
Yes - networks guarantee packets arrive in their original order.
